answer: The statutory rule is that “The registration of title to every land parcel under this Act shall be in accordance with the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.” Applied here, if the parcel is being brought under the title-registration system, the registration of title must follow the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.

When the Commissioner of Title Settlement receives the certified copies of cadastral maps, he must publish a Notice in the Gazette. That Notice must call for any claimants to the land parcel specified in the Notice to submit their claims to him within a prescribed period from the date of publication of the Notice. After claims are made in response to that Notice, the Commissioner of Title Settlement must cause an investigation to be conducted in order to determine the genuineness or otherwise of those claims. The rule therefore is: Gazette notice first, claims submitted within the prescribed period, and then an investigation into the claims.

The Act provides two different procedures:

1. **Referral of disputed claims for determination**: If, during investigations, the Commissioner of Title Settlement forms the opinion that, because of the disputed nature of the claims, it would be more appropriate for the investigations to be carried out by the District Court, the Commissioner of Title Settlement **may refer such claims for investigation and determination** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situate. This is a power of the Commissioner during the investigation stage. [21-1998/section-21]

2. **Claimant aggrieved by a declaration**: Any claimant who is aggrieved by a Declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14 may **prefer an appeal against such declaration within the prescribed period** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land parcel is situate. This is an appeal right given to the claimant after the declaration. [21-1998/section-22]

So, the first procedure is a discretionary referral by the Commissioner based on disputed claims during investigations, while the second is an appeal by an aggrieved claimant against the declaration within the prescribed period.

The governing rule is that a person acquiring an interest in a land parcel registered under the Act is not entitled to that title or interest unless it is registered under the Act. Also, a registered land parcel or any interest in it may be transferred or dealt with only in accordance with the Act, and “every disposition otherwise effected shall be void.” An instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the Act “shall take effect on registration” of that instrument under the Act.

Applied here, Nimal’s instrument was not registered under the Registration of Title Act. Therefore the transferee did not acquire the interest, and the private agreement alone did not make the transfer effective. The instrument would take legal effect only upon registration.

Section 48 provides that, except in accordance with the provisions of the Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under the Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common, “shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.” Applied here, the one instrument purporting to convey the parcel to two purchasers as owners in common is void and cannot be registered, unless it is made in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

The statutory rule is that, for lands or interests in land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a "First Class Title of Absolute Ownership" or a "Second Class Title of Ownership," "The Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) shall not apply" and "The Partition Act shall not apply."

Applied here, the parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership. Therefore, the Prescription Ordinance does not apply to that parcel, so ownership cannot be claimed through prescription under that provision. The Partition Act also does not apply to that parcel, so a partition action under that Act cannot be maintained in relation to it.

The statutory rule is:

- If the Superintendent of Surveys is satisfied that the condominium plan conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and the Registration of Title Act, he must certify the plan on behalf of the Surveyor-General and then: (a) file the original of the condominium plan after making a suitable reference on the cadastral map used for registration of title; and (b) forward the duplicate of the condominium plan and the application of the owner to the appropriate Registrar of Title.
- If the Registrar of Title is satisfied that the application conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and the Registration of Title Act, he must: (a) file the duplicate of the condominium plan in the Parcels File; (b) open a new title register in respect of each condominium parcel shown on the Condominium Plan and make suitable cross references to such register in the register in which the land parcel is registered; (c) record in the Property Section of the register pertaining to the land parcel that the land comprised therein consists only of common property; (d) record in the Encumbrances Section that registers in respect of condominium parcels have been opened; (e) inform the applicant that such condominium parcels have been registered and notify him of the reference numbers of the relevant registers; and (f) issue a Certificate of Title after recovery of the prescribed fees.

Applied to the facts, the condominium plan has been approved as conforming to the applicable laws, so the Superintendent’s next steps are to certify it, file the original after making the suitable cadastral-map reference, and send the duplicate and the owner’s application to the appropriate Registrar. The Registrar must then, if satisfied with the application, file the duplicate in the Parcels File, open the new title registers for each condominium parcel, make the required cross-references, record the common-property and encumbrance entries, notify the applicant of registration and the register numbers, and issue the Certificate of Title after taking the prescribed fees.

Rule: If a person dies intestate leaving a spouse, “the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property” of the deceased. Subject to that spouse’s right, inheritance passes in the order of (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals. As to descendants, “Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents”; “all the children take equally per capita,” but “the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.”

Application: Here, the estate is divided first into two equal parts because there is a surviving spouse.
- Surviving spouse = 1/2.
- The remaining 1/2 passes to descendants.

Among the descendants, there are two child-lines: (1) the living child, and (2) the predeceased child represented by two grandchildren. Because children and the issue of a deceased child take by representation, the remaining 1/2 is divided into 2 equal stirpes:
- 1/2 ÷ 2 = 1/4 for the living child’s share,
- 1/2 ÷ 2 = 1/4 for the deceased child’s share.

That deceased child’s 1/4 is then shared equally by the two grandchildren:
- 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8 each grandchild.

So the shares are:
- Surviving spouse: 1/2
- Living child: 1/4
- Each grandchild: 1/8

Order of succession applied: spouse first to one-half; then descendants take the remainder, with children and the children of a deceased child taking by representation.

The rule in s 5 is that every will made beyond the limits of Sri Lanka that contains a devise or disposition of immovable property situated within Sri Lanka is “valid and effectual to alienate and pass” that property if it has been “duly made and executed according to and in conformity with the forms and solemnities prescribed by the law of the country where” it was made and executed, and if the testator is “competent to make a will” by the law of that country or of Sri Lanka. Here, the will was executed outside Sri Lanka, it disposes of immovable property in Sri Lanka, it complies with the formalities of the country of execution, and the testator was competent under that country’s law. On those facts, the foreign will is capable of validly passing the Sri Lankan immovable property.

Before any precept or order for the service of notice or summons is issued in proceedings to enforce a right of pre-emption, the plaintiff must furnish proof to the court that the proceedings or action have been registered as a lis pendens in accordance with the Registration of Documents Ordinance. The court may also, at any time after the action is instituted, in its discretion order the plaintiff to deposit the purchase amount set out in the notice given under section 5. If the plaintiff defaults in depositing that amount within the period allowed by the court, or within further periods not exceeding three months in the aggregate, the action shall be struck off the roll of pending cases. [59-1947/section-10; 59-1947/section-11]

The statutory rule is that “[a] mortgage of a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot shall, if it is effected on or after the appointed day, be null and void notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law.” The Act’s “appointed day” is “the eleventh day of December, 1957.”

Applied here, the owner mortgages a physically divided portion of a tea estate as a separate lot after the appointed day. That is a mortgage of “a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot” effected on or after the appointed day, so the mortgage is null and void.

The rule is that “No share in the common elements” of a registered Condominium Property or registered Semi Condominium Property “shall be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of such property.” The same provision also says that “any alienation of any condominium parcel shall be deemed also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to that condominium parcel” even if the deed makes “no specific or particular reference” to that share.

Applied to the facts, the apartment owner cannot dispose of the share in the common elements separately while retaining the condominium parcel. If the condominium parcel itself is transferred, the undivided share in the common elements passes with it automatically, even without a specific reference in the transfer instrument.

The statutory rule is that “The Partition Law shall not apply to any land or building comprised in any registered Condominium Plan.” Applied here, the property is land and a building already comprised in a registered Condominium Plan, so the Partition Law does not apply to that property.

Under section 13, no plan or map, or copy or tracing of a plan or map, is receivable in evidence in any court in Sri Lanka unless it has been prepared in one of the statutory ways and properly certified.

The provision states that the plan or map must have been prepared "by or on behalf of the Surveyor-General by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him" and certified "by the Surveyor-General or by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him for such purpose," or else it must be "certified by a registered licensed surveyor."

So, a land plan prepared by a surveyor is receivable only if it satisfies the statutory preparation and certification requirement in section 13: either the Surveyor-General route described above, or certification by a registered licensed surveyor.

Yes. A cadastral map, plan, or any other plan or map prepared in accordance with any written law, if it purports to be a true copy and purports to be signed by the Surveyor-General or any officer acting on his behalf, is “admissible evidence in all cases and for all purposes instead of the original.” It may initially be taken as “prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated there in as being that of the original,” until evidence to the contrary is given. The provision also says it is not necessary to prove that the copy was in fact signed or authenticated by the Surveyor-General or such officer, or that it is a true copy, or that the facts reflected are accurate, until evidence to the contrary has first been given.

The statutory rule is that it “shall not be lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares … unless a proper instrument of transfer has been delivered to the company.” So, on these facts, the company may not register the voluntary transfer because no proper instrument of transfer has been delivered.

The exception is that “nothing in this section shall affect any power of the company to register as shareholder … any person to whom the right of any shares … has been transmitted by operation of law.” So, where entitlement to the shares passes by operation of law, the company’s power to register that person as shareholder is preserved even without the ordinary instrument of transfer.

Under Companies Act, s 79, “A certificate signed under the name of the company by a director and secretary of the company specifying any shares held by any shareholder, shall be prima facie evidence of the title of the shareholder to the shares.”

Applied here, a share certificate signed in the company’s name by a director and the secretary, and specifying the shares held by the shareholder, is prima facie evidence that the recorded shareholder has title to those shares. That means the certificate is evidence of title unless rebutted.

The statutory duties breached are:

1. Under s 188, a director “shall not act or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes ... the provisions contained in the articles of the company.”
2. Under s 189(a), a person exercising powers or performing duties as a director “shall not act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent.”
3. Under s 189(b), such a person “shall exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience.”

Applied to the facts: the director approved conduct that breaches the company’s articles, so that breaches s 188. The director then carried out the decision recklessly, so that breaches s 189(a). The director also failed to exercise the skill and care reasonably expected from a person with that director’s knowledge and experience, so that breaches s 189(b).

Under section 25, "alienation" means "transfer, lease or mortgage of lands situated within Sri Lanka". Under section 18, "Any alienation of land effected in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be void and shall have no effect in law." Applied here, a transfer of land completed in direct contravention of the Act is an alienation, and its legal effect is that it is void and has no effect in law.
